lines.text: Your agent works in a terminal. Your team talks in Slack. And you sit in the middle, copying messages back and forth.
A teammate reports a bug in Slack, so you paste it into the terminal. The agent asks a question, so you paste that back. All day.
Agent R Q connects any agent to your workspace with one M C P config. Your team can hand it work, and approve what it does, right from Slack.
Every agent has its own setup: its own files, its own flags, its own docs.
In Agent R Q, every workspace has a Setup tab. Ada opens storefront's, and picks her agent: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, or any A C P agent.
Step one is the same for all of them: an M C P config with this workspace's address and token. She copies it into the project, as dot M C P dot json.
For Claude Code, step two allows the workspace's tools, so Claude doesn't stop to ask about each one.
Then one start command. Claude Code opens with the workspace as a channel, so new tasks reach it on their own. No polling.
Codex and Antigravity connect through the Agent R Q gateway: one command, sign in once, and they join the same way.
Claude Code and Cursor also have an Agent R Q plugin. And with a machine enrolled, she can skip all of this and start the agent from the browser.
Once it's connected, the agent has seven tools: tasks, memory, skills, the workspace, site tools, the Pano, and help.
Ada gives it a real task: the order export times out on big stores, so stream it instead. The agent picks it up and marks it as ongoing.
It works in the repo, and reports back on the task, with the test output attached.
When it needs a decision, it asks: should the export include cancelled orders? Ada answers on the task, and the agent carries on.
What it learns goes into the workspace's memory and skills, so the next agent starts where this one stopped.
No agent at all? The agent R Q dash W S command has the same tools. A C I job can open a task, or reply with a log file.
But Ada's team doesn't live in Agent R Q. They live in Slack.
In the workspace settings, she clicks Add to Slack and approves the app. Agent R Q creates a private channel for this workspace, and invites her.
She invites Sam, who's on call this week.
Now every new task posts to that channel as its own thread. Every message on the task lands in the same thread.
Sam hands the agent work without leaving Slack: slash T, a title, and a description. If the agent is free, it starts right away.
To steer it, Sam mentions the bot in the thread. The agent gets that as a reply on the task, files included.
Ada sees the whole conversation in the browser, on the same task, marked as coming from Slack.
When the agent wants to run a command that needs approval, the request posts in the thread, with Allow and Deny.
Sam clicks Allow. The agent carries on, and the buttons turn into one line: allowed by Sam.
If Ada answers in the browser first, the thread says so instead. Nobody answers the same request twice.
Each visit to the Setup tab makes a new token, good for a year. It works for this one workspace, and no other.
If a token leaks, Reset Workspace ID gives the workspace a new address, and every old token stops working.
Every request from Slack must carry Slack's signature, and old ones are turned away.
One thing to know: anyone in that channel can approve. So the channel's members are your approvers. Keep the list short.
One config connects any agent. Seven tools let it work with you. And your team hands it work, and approves it, from Slack.
Which tool should Agent R Q plug into next? Tell us in the comments, and try it at Agent R Q dot com.
